overview: Caddo peoples built distinct river-valley communities linked by language, kinship and exchange. House traces, a surviving canoe and pottery reveal skilled work alongside farming and ceremonial life. Colonial dispossession forced major movements, but Caddo people continued and today sustain the Caddo Nation and renewed artistic traditions.

periods.title: Distinct local Caddo communities
periods.summary: Late Caddo communities developed varied local ceramic and settlement traditions. Farming, exchange and ceremonial centers connected people without making them a single uniform kingdom. These approximate phases describe cultural change.

periods.title: Contact and colonial pressure
periods.summary: The Spanish expedition led by Moscoso crossed Caddo lands in 1542. Later French and Spanish trade and settlement brought new goods, competition and disease. Caddo groups negotiated these changes through their own communities and alliances.

periods.title: Forced cession and repeated displacement
periods.summary: The 1835 land cession and settler pressure pushed Caddo families from earlier homes. A period on the Brazos reservation ended with another forced move to Indian Territory in 1859.

periods.title: Continuity through displacement
periods.summary: Life in Indian Territory and later Oklahoma involved rebuilding after dispossession. Caddo people continue through their Nation, education and artistic work, including the renewal of pottery-making knowledge.

items.text: At the George C. Davis site in east Texas, excavators found overlapping post patterns left by wooden buildings. Radiocarbon evidence places the main community between the ninth and early fourteenth centuries. Buildings were repeatedly renewed as people lived around ceremonial mounds.

A magnetic survey detected structures invisible on the surface. Excavation in 2003 confirmed one large building with a central hearth and four internal roof supports. The pattern reveals engineering and interior space, although it does not identify every activity or occupant.

A dugout canoe eroding from a Red River bluff in northwestern Louisiana was radiocarbon dated to about 1000 CE. The surviving wooden vessel gives direct evidence of water transport beyond later written descriptions.

Late-seventeenth-century accounts describe corn stored in raised granaries, seed kept for planting and dried beans, squash and fruit. Storage helped households bridge seasonal shortages. These accounts mainly concern Hasinai communities and cannot describe every Caddo settlement.

Housebuilding, planting and harvest brought people together. Maternal kinship connected households, while chiefs consulted community elders. Such relationships organized practical work as well as public decisions.

Caddo potters built vessels by joining coils of prepared clay to a base, then thinning and smoothing the walls. Temper mixed into clay and controlled drying helped a vessel survive manufacture and firing. Cooking pots and decorated bottles required different choices of shape and finish.

Engraved designs cut across a vessel's surface, unlike incised lines pressed into damp clay. Researchers and potters debate whether some ancient engraving occurred before or after firing. Modern experiments illuminate the skill without proving one method was universal.

Jereldine Redcorn's 1998 bottle Taysha has hollow tripod feet containing clay balls that rattle. Its form joins visual pattern with sound. It is a documented modern artwork drawing on ancestral pottery, not an excavated ancient vessel.

Redcorn learned through study, experiment and conversations with archaeologists when there was no local group of elder potters to teach her. Her work shows renewal as active investigation and artistic choice, not simply copying old designs.
The 1835 cession forced Caddo groups from lands in present Louisiana and Arkansas. Families moved toward Texas and, in some cases, Mexico. The agreement did not give them a secure replacement home.

In 1859, renewed pressure forced people from the Brazos reservation to Indian Territory. They left cultivated land and family graves behind. This was a rupture in community life, not the disappearance of Caddo people.

The Caddo Nation's education services include cultural learning and vocational support. These are contemporary institutions serving people with changing needs, alongside the continued importance of language, arts and family histories.

ending.text: Caddo communities endured repeated dispossession, including the forced move of 1859. The Caddo Nation and Caddo cultural life continue. The end of an imported map interval is not an extinction date, and the many earlier communities should not be treated as a single kingdom with one fall.
